summary: This chapter teaches you to read the road before anyone says a word. Signs, traffic lights, and lines painted on the pavement all send messages through shape and color. If you learn what each shape and color means, you can answer many test questions even when you cannot read the words on a sign.

The shape of a sign tells you a lot. An eight-sided red sign always means stop, and a red and white triangle pointing down means yield. Yellow diamonds warn you about a hazard ahead, orange signs mark a work zone, and a five-sided sign warns of a school zone. White rectangles show rules you must obey, such as speed limits, and blue signs point to services like gas, food, or a hospital.

Traffic lights have steady and flashing versions. A steady yellow light means the light is about to turn red, so stop if you can do it safely. A flashing red light works like a stop sign, and a flashing yellow light means slow down and go with care. If the lights are dark because of a power failure, treat the intersection as a four-way stop.

Pavement lines follow a simple color rule. Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions, and white lines separate lanes going the same way. A solid line on your side means you may not cross it to pass, while a broken line means you may pass when it is safe.

concepts.definition: An eight-sided (octagon) red sign means you must come to a full stop, then go only when the way is clear. A red and white triangle pointing down means slow down and let other traffic and pedestrians go first, stopping if needed.
concepts.tip: Stop has eight sides, the most of any sign. Yield is the only sign that points down.

concepts.definition: Yellow means warning, orange means work zone, white means a rule you must obey, green gives directions, blue points to driver services, and brown points to parks and recreation areas.
concepts.tip: Orange is the color of traffic cones, so think 'road work'. Blue is for services you need on a trip.

concepts.definition: A diamond warns of a hazard ahead. A five-sided (pentagon) sign warns of a school zone or school crossing. A tall or wide rectangle shows a rule or gives directions.
concepts.tip: A pentagon looks like a little house with a roof, and a schoolhouse is where kids are.

concepts.definition: A flashing red light means stop completely, then go when it is safe, just like a stop sign. A flashing yellow light means slow down and pass through with extra care. You do not have to stop for a flashing yellow.
concepts.tip: Flashing red = stop sign. Flashing yellow = caution sign.

concepts.definition: A steady yellow light warns that the light is about to turn red, so stop if you can do it safely. A green arrow means you may turn in that direction because oncoming traffic is stopped, but still yield to anyone already in the intersection.
concepts.tip: Yellow is a warning to get ready to stop, not a signal to speed up.

concepts.definition: Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes moving the same way. A solid line on your side means do not cross it to pass. A broken line means passing is allowed when it is safe. Two solid yellow lines mean no passing for either side.
concepts.tip: Look only at the line closest to you: solid means stay, broken means you may go around.

concepts.definition: If the traffic lights at an intersection are not working because of a power failure and no officer is directing traffic, treat it as a four-way stop. Every driver stops, then goes in turn.
concepts.tip: No lights means everyone stops, just like a four-way stop sign.

points: Tests often show a sign shape with no words. Know octagon (stop), triangle (yield), diamond (warning), and pentagon (school).
A flashing yellow light does not require a stop. Do not mix it up with a flashing red light.
Trap: a broken yellow line on the other side does not let you pass if the solid line is on your side.
Orange signs are for work zones, not general warnings. Yellow is for general warnings.
When lights are dark, the answer is to treat the intersection as a four-way stop, not to drive through.

summary: This chapter covers who goes first when paths cross, and how to make turns the right way. Right of way is never something you take; the law only says who must yield. The goal is always to avoid a crash, so even when the other driver should yield, be ready to let them go.

At a four-way stop, the vehicle that stopped first goes first. If two vehicles stop at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. When you turn left on a green light with no arrow, you must yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians in the crosswalk. Drivers coming out of a private driveway yield to traffic on the road, and drivers merging from an entrance ramp yield to highway traffic.

Some road users always come first. Stop for pedestrians in a crosswalk, and always stop for a person using a white cane or a guide dog. When an emergency vehicle comes with its siren and lights on, pull to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes. Let a funeral procession led by an escort finish going through, even if your light is green.

Turns follow simple lane rules. Make a right turn from the right lane into the right lane, and watch for bicycles in a bike lane on your right. In Florida you may turn right on a steady red light after a full stop, unless a sign says no. You may also turn left on red from a one-way street onto another one-way street going left, after a full stop. In a roundabout, traffic moves counterclockwise, and drivers entering yield to traffic already in the circle.

concepts.definition: The first vehicle to come to a full stop is the first to go. If two vehicles stop at the same time, the driver on the left lets the driver on the right go first.
concepts.tip: First come, first served. In a tie, 'right goes first'.

concepts.term: Left turn on a green light
concepts.definition: On a steady green light with no arrow, you may turn left only after you let oncoming traffic and pedestrians in the crosswalk go first. Wait inside the intersection only when it is safe to do so.
concepts.tip: A green ball is not a green arrow. Without an arrow, oncoming cars still have the right of way.

concepts.definition: When a police car, fire truck, or ambulance comes toward you with its siren and flashing lights on, pull over to the right edge of the road and stop. Stay stopped until it has passed. Do not stop inside an intersection.
concepts.tip: Hear a siren, think 'pull right and stop'.

concepts.definition: Stop for pedestrians in a marked crosswalk. A person carrying a white cane or walking with a guide dog always has the right of way, and you must stop and let them cross.
concepts.tip: A white cane or guide dog means you stop, every time.

concepts.definition: After a full stop, you may turn right on a steady red light unless a sign forbids it. You may also turn left on red from a one-way street onto another one-way street that moves left. Always yield to pedestrians and cross traffic first.
concepts.tip: Red-light turns are allowed only after a full stop, and only right, or left from one-way into one-way.

concepts.definition: A round intersection where all traffic moves counterclockwise around a center island. Drivers entering the circle must yield to vehicles already inside it. Never stop inside the circle unless you must avoid a crash.
concepts.tip: In a roundabout, the cars already circling have the right of way.

concepts.definition: For a right turn, start in the right lane and finish in the right lane. For a left turn from a one-way street onto another one-way street, start in the far left lane and finish in the left lane. Check for bicycles in a bike lane before turning right across it.
concepts.tip: Turn from the closest lane into the closest lane.

points: Four-way stop ties are a favorite question: the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
When turning left on a plain green light, you yield to oncoming traffic. Many people forget this.
For a siren, the answer is to pull to the right and stop, not to speed up or stop in the middle of the lane.
Drivers leaving a driveway or entering from a ramp must yield to the traffic already on the road.
A funeral procession with an escort keeps going through the intersection even after your light turns green.

summary: This chapter is full of numbers: speed limits, signaling distance, and how far you must park from things like fire hydrants and crosswalks. These numbers are easy to mix up, so it helps to learn them as one short list and review it often.

Florida sets default speed limits that apply when no sign says otherwise: 30 mph in business or residential areas and 55 mph on other roads. Limited access highways, such as interstates, may be posted up to 70 mph. On interstates with four or more lanes, the minimum speed is 40 mph, or 50 mph where the posted limit is 70 mph. Above all, the basic speed rule says you must drive slower than the limit when rain, fog, or traffic makes the posted speed unsafe.

Before any turn, signal for at least the last 100 feet. Normally pass on the left, and never pass within 100 feet of a railroad crossing. When you pass a bicycle, leave at least 3 feet of space. When someone passes you, do not speed up.

Parking rules keep safety equipment and views clear. Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet of a stop sign or traffic light on your approach, or within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing. You may never stop or park inside an intersection, on a crosswalk, or on a sidewalk.

concepts.definition: When no sign shows a different limit, the speed limit is 30 mph in business or residential areas and 55 mph on all other roads. Limited access highways, such as interstates, may be posted as high as 70 mph.
concepts.tip: Think '30 in town, 55 out of town, 70 tops on the interstate'.

concepts.definition: On interstate highways with four or more lanes, you must drive at least 40 mph. Where the posted limit is 70 mph, the minimum is 50 mph. This applies only when conditions are safe.
concepts.tip: Minimum is 40, but a 70 mph road raises it to 50.

concepts.definition: You may never drive faster than is safe for the conditions, even if the sign shows a higher number. In heavy rain, fog, or thick traffic, slow down below the posted limit.
concepts.tip: The posted limit is the top speed for perfect conditions, not a target.

concepts.definition: You must signal your turn or lane change continuously for at least the last 100 feet before you turn.
concepts.tip: 100 feet is about the length of six or seven cars.

concepts.definition: Pass on the left when the road ahead is clear and passing is allowed. Do not pass within 100 feet of a railroad crossing or intersection. Leave at least 3 feet when you pass a bicycle. When you are being passed, do not speed up.
concepts.tip: Two numbers: 100 feet from a crossing, 3 feet from a bike.

concepts.definition: Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, 30 feet of a stop sign, flashing signal, or traffic light on your approach, or 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.
concepts.tip: Hydrant 15, crosswalk 20, stop sign 30, railroad 50. The numbers grow as the danger grows.

concepts.definition: You may not stop, stand, or park inside an intersection, on a crosswalk, or on a sidewalk, even for a moment.
concepts.tip: If people walk on it or cars cross through it, do not park on it.

points: Parking distance questions swap the numbers 15, 20, 30, and 50. Match each to the right object.
30 mph and 55 mph are the defaults. Choices like 25 mph or 35 mph are common traps.
Minimum speed on a 70 mph interstate is 50 mph, but 40 mph elsewhere on four-lane interstates.
If a question mentions rain or fog, the answer is usually 'slower than the posted limit'.
Signal for at least 100 feet before a turn, not 50 feet.

summary: This chapter is about driving safely when things are not perfect: at night, in rain, during a blowout, and around vehicles that need extra room. Many questions in this area ask about school buses and the Move Over law, where one small detail changes the answer.

Turn on your headlights from sunset to sunrise and any time rain, smoke, or fog makes it hard to see, even in daytime. Switch from high beams to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet, or when you are within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following. If a front tire blows out, hold the wheel firmly, keep the car straight, and ease off the gas before braking gently.

When a school bus stops with its stop signal out, traffic in both directions must stop and stay stopped until the signal is pulled back. The only exception is for drivers on the other side of a divided highway with a raised median, a physical barrier, or an unpaved median at least 5 feet wide. A painted center turn lane does not count as a divider.

Florida's Move Over law protects people working on the roadside. When you see a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck, service vehicle, or disabled vehicle with flashing lights or hazards, move out of the lane next to it if it is safe. If you cannot move over, slow to 20 mph below the posted limit, or to 5 mph when the limit is 20 mph or less. At railroad crossings, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail when a train is coming, and never drive around lowered gates.

concepts.definition: Use headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever rain, smoke, or fog makes it hard to see. Dim your high beams when an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet, and when you are within 300 feet behind another vehicle.
concepts.tip: 500 for cars coming at you, 300 for cars in front of you.

concepts.definition: When a school bus shows its stop signal, drivers in both directions must stop and wait until the signal is withdrawn. Drivers on the other side of a divided highway do not have to stop only if the median is raised, is a physical barrier, or is unpaved and at least 5 feet wide.
concepts.tip: Both ways stop, unless something solid or grassy 5 feet wide is between you.

concepts.definition: For a stopped emergency vehicle, tow truck, service vehicle, or disabled vehicle showing flashing lights, hazards, flares, or warning signs, move out of the lane next to it if safe. If you cannot, slow to 20 mph below the posted limit, or to 5 mph when the limit is 20 mph or less.
concepts.tip: Move over, or slow down by 20. On a 20 mph street, crawl at 5.

concepts.definition: When a train is coming, stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail. Never drive through, around, or under a gate that is down or moving, even if you do not see a train.
concepts.tip: Stop in the 15 to 50 foot zone. Gates down means wait, always.

concepts.definition: If a tire suddenly blows out, grip the steering wheel firmly and keep the car going straight. Ease off the gas and let the car slow down, then brake gently and pull off the road.
concepts.tip: Hold tight, foot off the gas, brake last.

concepts.definition: Large trucks have big blind spots beside them, close behind them, and close in front of them. If you cannot see the truck driver's face in the truck's side mirror, the driver probably cannot see you.
concepts.tip: No face in the mirror means you are invisible to the driver.

points: A painted center turn lane is not a divider. Traffic in both directions still stops for a school bus.
Move Over math: subtract 20 from the posted limit. On a 55 mph road, slow to 35 mph or less.
The Move Over law now also covers ordinary disabled cars with hazard lights on, not only police and tow trucks.
Dimming distances: 500 feet for oncoming traffic, 300 feet when following.
Lowered railroad gates mean stop and wait, even if you see no train.

summary: This chapter covers the rules for getting and keeping a Florida license, plus the laws on seat belts, phones, alcohol, and crashes. Teen license steps and alcohol limits come with exact numbers, so learn them carefully.

You can get a learner license at age 15. A learner must always drive with a licensed driver age 21 or older in the front passenger seat. For the first three months, a learner may drive only in daylight, and after that until 10 p.m. To get a Class E license, a teen must hold the learner license for 12 months (or until turning 18) and log 50 practice hours, 10 of them at night. A 16-year-old with a license may not drive alone from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., and a 17-year-old from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m., unless with a licensed driver 21 or older or driving to or from work.

It is illegal to drive with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.08% or more, and for drivers under 21 the limit is 0.02%. By driving in Florida you agree to a lawful breath, blood, or urine test. Refusing for the first time brings a one-year license suspension, and refusing again brings 18 months.

The driver, the front seat passenger, and every passenger under 18 must wear a seat belt. Children 5 and younger must ride in a federally approved child restraint. Texting while driving is a primary offense, so an officer can stop you for it alone, and in school zones and active work zones you may use a phone only hands-free. After a minor crash with only property damage, move your car out of traffic if it is safe, then stay and exchange information.

concepts.definition: Available at age 15. A licensed driver age 21 or older must always sit in the front passenger seat. During the first three months you may drive only in daylight. After three months you may drive until 10 p.m.
concepts.tip: 15 to start, 21 beside you, daylight for 3 months, then until 10.

concepts.term: Moving up to a Class E license
concepts.definition: A teen must hold a learner license for 12 months with no traffic convictions, or until age 18 if that comes first. A parent or adult 21 or older must certify at least 50 hours of driving practice, with 10 of those hours at night.
concepts.tip: 12 months, 50 hours, 10 at night.

concepts.definition: A 16-year-old with a license may not drive between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. A 17-year-old may not drive between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. Both are allowed if a licensed driver 21 or older is with them or they are driving to or from work.
concepts.tip: 16 is home by 11. 17 gets two more hours, until 1.

concepts.definition: Driving with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.08% or more is DUI. For drivers under 21, it is illegal to drive with a level of 0.02% or more. You can still be charged at a lower level if alcohol has affected your driving.
concepts.tip: Adults: 0.08. Under 21: 0.02, which is close to zero.

source.org: Florida Statutes, Chapter 316 (s. 316.193); Florida Driver License Handbook

concepts.definition: By driving in Florida, you agree to take a lawful breath, blood, or urine test if arrested for DUI. A first refusal leads to a one-year license suspension. A refusal after an earlier refusal leads to an 18-month suspension.
concepts.tip: First no = 1 year. Second no = 18 months.

concepts.definition: The driver, the front seat passenger, and all passengers under 18 must wear seat belts. Children 5 and younger must use a federally approved child restraint. Children through age 3 need a separate carrier or built-in child seat, and ages 4 and 5 may use a booster seat.
concepts.tip: Front seat always buckles. Under 18 always buckles. 5 and under needs a child seat.

concepts.definition: Texting, emailing, and messaging while driving are banned, and it is a primary offense, so you can be stopped for it alone. In a school zone, school crossing, or active work zone, you may not hold a phone at all and may use it only hands-free.
concepts.tip: Never text. In school and work zones, hands off the phone.

points: Alcohol limits: 0.08% for drivers 21 and older, 0.02% for drivers under 21. Choices like 0.05% are traps.
Teen curfew hours are often swapped: 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. at 16, and 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. at 17.
The learner's supervising driver must be 21 or older and sit in the front passenger seat, at all hours.
A first test refusal means a 1-year suspension, not 6 months.
Texting is a primary offense: an officer can stop you for texting alone.
